5. Historical Data Collection

The observed data set was developed by analyzing minimum daily temperature records from COOP weather stations throughout the CONUS. COOP stations generally measure temperature at least hourly, and they record the minimum temperature for each 24-hour time span. Cooperative observers include state universities, state and federal agencies, and private individuals whose stations are managed and maintained by NWS. Observers are trained to collect data, and the NWS provides and maintains standard equipment to gather these data. Data collected by COOP sites are referred to as U.S. Daily Surface Data or Summary of the Day data.

This indicator uses approximately 597 stations that met criteria for data availability; each station had to have less than 10 percent of temperature data missing over the period from 1895 to 2023. Temperature monitoring procedures are described in the full metadata for the COOP data set. General information on COOP weather data can also be found at this link.

6. Indicator Derivation

This pairing defines the length of the growing season as the period between the last spring frost and the first fall frost. The resulting length in days is presented as an anomaly, which represents the difference between an observed value and the corresponding value from a baseline period. This feature uses a baseline period of 1895–2023, so annual values are being compared against a long-term mean for the full observed period of record.

Observed Data

Minimum daily temperature data from the COOP data set were used to determine the dates of last spring frost and first fall frost at each weather station using an inclusive threshold of 32°F. Methods for producing state, regional, and national values by year were designed to weight all areas evenly, regardless of station density. Anomalies were calculated relative to the full period mean. Kunkel et al. (2004) provides a complete description of the analytical procedures used.

For the maps, the project team calculated total change over the observed period by multiplying each state’s linear regression slope by the length of the period.

Model Outputs

The project team performed the following steps via R scripts:

  • For each downscaled model, the team used the “tasmin” variable with daily GCM outputs to calculate the length of each year’s growing season for each grid cell.
  • The project team converted each year’s growing season to an anomaly, initially using 1951–2000 as the reference point because the models do not provide outputs back to 1895 like EPA’s observed baseline.
  • For each year, the project team calculated an average anomaly for the CONUS and for each state by averaging grid cells proportional to their area—thus accounting for pixels that are only partially within the border of the geographic area of interest.
  • In performing these calculations, the project team applied a coastline mask to crop mixed land/ocean pixels. The team also excluded the Great Lakes from the calculations.
  • The team aggregated the 16 models using the standard Bayesian model weighting approach used in the Fifth National Climate Assessment and documented by Massoud et al. (2023).
  • The team smoothed modeled results using an 11-year moving average. The team performed this step independently for the hindcast (through 2014) and for each scenario from 2015 (the first year of divergence) forward.
  • The team calculated total change for the 2021–2100 period for each scenario on the maps via linear regression slope multiplied by the length of the period.

7. Alignment

To ensure consistency in how the anomalies are defined, the project team had to ensure that the observed and modeled anomalies were all presented relative to a common baseline. The observed CONUS anomalies for the graph had already been calculated with respect to an 1895–2023 baseline, as shown in the Length of Growing Season indicator. Downscaled model outputs were only available back to 1950, so the modeled anomalies were initially calculated relative to a standard 50-year baseline period: 1951–2000. The project team then shifted the model outputs vertically on the graph such that the 1951–2000 mean for the model hindcast would match the 1895–2023 mean for the observed time series. This aligns the model outputs with the observed anomalies that remain based on an 1895–2023 baseline. The alignment of baseline here is essentially just a vertical shift on the graph, not a change to the shape of the time series.

The results show good alignment. Thus, no other transformation was necessary.

8. Display

The interactive graph for this pairing shows the following elements:

  • Observed data from EPA’s indicator from 1895 to 2023.
  • Modeled hindcast from 1950 to 2014. The line on the graph shows the Bayesian weighted average of the 16 GCMs, smoothed using an 11-year moving average. The resulting 11-year means are plotted from 1955 to 2009, as the project team did not attempt to apply any endpoint padding at either end of the series.
  • Modeled projections from 2015 to 2100 for four emissions scenarios (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5), with 2014 added for continuity (2014 is the last year before the scenarios diverge). Each scenario line on the graph shows the Bayesian weighted average of the 16 GCMs, smoothed using an 11-year moving average. The resulting 11-year means are plotted starting at 2014 to provide continuity with the hindcast annual ranges, although the scenarios do not start to diverge until 2015. Smoothed values for 2014–2019 pick up some hindcast years in the average. The 11-year means are plotted through 2095, including data from 2090 through 2100, the last year of available data. Scenarios have been assigned “plain-language” names for consistency throughout this pairings effort.
  • A shaded band around each of the scenarios reflects the 10th to 90th percentiles among the 16 models. This shaded band therefore illustrates the range of modeled values. The shaded bands show annual values; they have not been smoothed. The projected ranges start in 2014 to provide continuity with the hindcast, but the scenarios begin to diverge in 2015.

The interactive maps show:

  • Total observed change from 1895 to 2023.
  • Total projected change from 2024 to 2100 for four emissions scenarios (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5). Each scenario shows the Bayesian weighted average of the 16 GCMs.

9. Quality Assurance and Quality Control

The technical documentation for the Length of Growing Season indicator provides details about specific quality measures employed in collecting and compiling COOP weather station data, ensuring the quality of digitization of older records, and identifying and eliminating outliers when assembling the final observed data set. Quality procedures for each GCM (e.g., validation) are described in source papers published by the organizations that have developed and run each model; they are available through links in the overall technical documentation for this effort. For each pairing, the project team conducted typical quality control steps, including independently checking all aggregations, unit conversions, transformations, and other calculations.
